title: How to Read This Book
text:
## How to Read This Book

This is a documentary book. It tells the story of one long argument inside an elected public board: whether a hospital commissioner could make his own audio recording of the board's open public meetings. The argument began at Matt Ready's first regular meeting in March 2014 and was formally settled by a unanimous board vote in January 2021. Its after-effects were still being discussed at a board retreat years later.

Every quotation in this book is copied word for word from a file in the author's archive. Nothing has been reconstructed, smoothed, or improved. Auto-generated transcripts keep their errors ("Council" for counsel, "Mr. Reddy" for Mr. Ready, broken sentences), because correcting them would mean guessing what was said. Where a passage is cut, the cut is marked with an ellipsis (…), and most of those ellipses were already in the source compilation.

The narrative between the quotations is editorial. It sets the scene and connects the documents. It is not evidence, and it does not add facts that are not in the sources.

## Source labels

Each document or excerpt is introduced with a label telling you what kind of record it is. The difference matters, because a transcript, a letter written that week, and a memory written ten years later are not the same kind of evidence.

- **TRANSCRIPT** — words taken from an audio recording of a meeting, as transcribed in the author's 2023 compilation or his 2023 blog post. Closest to what was actually said.
- **DOCUMENT** — a letter, email, policy text, or legal opinion excerpt, as reproduced in the author's archive.
- **AUTHOR'S ACCOUNT (CONTEMPORANEOUS)** — Matt Ready writing at or near the time of the events, such as his July 2, 2016 blog post or the first-person notes in the 2023 compilation.
- **AUTHOR'S RECOLLECTION (LATER)** — Matt Ready describing events years afterward: the 2025 op-ed, 2025 emails, the 2026 bar-grievance narrative, the September 2026 Chelan addendum. These are his memory and his characterization, not transcripts.
- **SECONDARY** — a summary or quotation that appears only in the author's later analytical writing (Section 3E.1 of his 2026 manuscript), where the underlying transcript excerpt is not in the files used for this book.

## What this book does not do

It does not reveal hospital confidential information. Nothing from executive sessions is included except what the author has already published. It does not quote any legal opinion that is not already quoted in the archive. The 2016 written opinion from district counsel is described only as the people in these records describe it. Its text is not in the files used for this book.

Characterizations of other people's motives ("deception," "fraud," "stalling") are the author's opinions, marked as his. The other side of the argument is given in the other people's own recorded words wherever the record has them, especially in Chapter 9, where the CEO and other commissioners explain their views.

title: Cast of Characters
text:
## Cast of Characters

People are listed in the order they enter the story. Titles are as of the events described. Spellings follow the most common form in the sources; variants are noted.

**Matt Ready** (Matthew Ready) — Author. Commissioner, Position 3, Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2 (Jefferson Healthcare). A hospital employee for about fifteen years in Information Systems and Performance Improvement, he first won the commissioner seat in the November 2013 election and took office in January 2014. Re-elected since; still serving as of 2026. He is the commissioner who recorded.

**Marie Dressler** — Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare. Board chair in March 2014, when she recessed the meeting over the recorder. Still on the board at the Port Ludlow retreat, where the transcript lists her as "Commissioner Dressler" and the facilitator sometimes calls her "Mari." She remembered knowing Ready about 25 years earlier, when she was nursing and he "was working in it."

**Jill Buhler** (later **Jill Buhler Rienstra**) — Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare. Excused from the March 19, 2014 meeting. Present at Chelan in 2016. Board chair in later years (the source that says she "found the opinion on her desk" refers to her as chair). Listed as "Commissioner Buhler Rienstra" in the Port Ludlow transcript, where she apologizes to Ready.

**Mike Glenn** — Chief Executive Officer of Jefferson Healthcare throughout the period. In March 2014 he relayed what he described as counsel's recommendation that a board member not record. In 2016 he obtained a written opinion from the district's law firm. At the Port Ludlow retreat he gives his own account of why he sought that letter.

**Tony DeLeo** (also spelled De Leo, Deleo) — Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare. In 2014 he told the chair Ready had stopped recording. At Chelan in 2016 he told Ready, "We're not going to record this meeting," and walked out. In the 2016 blog post Ready says he rejoined later.

**Brad Berg** — Attorney. The district's outside counsel. His firm was Foster Pepper at the time of the early events (as identified in the author's later writing) and later Foster Garvey. According to Ready's account, Glenn and Dressler consulted him in 2014, Ready reached him by phone, and his firm wrote the 2016 opinion. He does not speak in any transcript in this book.

**Kees Kolff** — Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare. At Chelan in 2016 he said, "There should be an official record if it's an official meeting." At Port Ludlow he apologized for not backing Ready up more. (Ready's 2025 op-ed credits "the arrival of two new commissioners—Kolff and McComas" with helping end the dispute, yet the 2016 transcript already shows Kolff on the board. The sources do not reconcile this.)

**Karma Bass** — Governance consultant, Via Healthcare Consulting. Appears in transcripts as "Consultant Karma B." She facilitated the October 14, 2019 retreat and the Port Ludlow retreat. She was hired again in 2025, after this book's story ends.

**John French** — Attorney who advised the board at the December 18, 2019 meeting. He told the board he did not know whether a board member could record over other members' objections. Ready later said that French promised to work on the question and that Ready never heard from him again. His firm and formal title are not in the source files.

**Bruce McComas** — Commissioner, Jefferson Healthcare. He says in the Port Ludlow transcript that he came on the board in 2018, after the 2014 and 2016 incidents, and that the 2021 policy settled the matter for him.

Others are named only in passing: "Laurie" (addressed once by the facilitator in the Port Ludlow transcript; not otherwise identified), and Ready's colleague "Bruce" (McComas), whom Ready refers to in the same transcript.

## Organizations and Legal Notes

Every organization mentioned in this book, with its full name and legal character. Where the source files do not state an organization's legal form, this section says so rather than guessing. The few items that rely on general public knowledge rather than the archive are marked *(general reference)*.

## Public bodies

**Jefferson County Public Hospital District No. 2** — *Doing business as Jefferson Healthcare.* A public hospital district organized under Washington law (RCW chapter 70.44) and a municipal corporation of the State of Washington, serving eastern Jefferson County. Its main hospital is in Port Townsend. It is governed by an elected five-member Board of Commissioners. Ready's 2026 bar narrative describes it as "a Washington public hospital district and municipal corporation." As a public agency it is bound by the Open Public Meetings Act and the Public Records Act. The transcripts also call it "Public Hospital District N.2," "the district," and "the organization."

**Board of Commissioners, Jefferson Healthcare** — The district's governing body: five commissioners elected by position (Ready holds Position 3). It acts only by majority vote in a properly noticed open public meeting. It is not a separate legal entity from the district.

**Office of the Washington State Attorney General** — An executive-branch agency of the State of Washington. It issued Attorney General Opinion AGO 1998 No. 15, which Ready attached to his March 26, 2014 letter. Formal AG opinions are advisory interpretations of state law. They are not court rulings, but Washington courts and agencies routinely give them weight *(general reference)*.

**Washington State Bar Association (WSBA)** — The statutory body that licenses and disciplines Washington lawyers under the authority of the Washington Supreme Court *(general reference for legal form)*. It enters this story only at the end: Ready's 2025 and June 25, 2026 grievances about attorney Brad Berg include the 2014–2021 recording episode as background.

**Olympic Medical Center (OMC)** — Clallam County Public Hospital District No. 2, a separate Washington public hospital district and municipal corporation *(legal name: general reference)*. Mentioned only in the Afterword, as the other party in the 2025 Peninsula Health Alliance dispute.

## Private organizations

**Foster Pepper PLLC / Foster Garvey PC** — A private Seattle-based law firm and the employer of district counsel Brad Berg. The author's writing names the firm "Foster Pepper" for the 2014 period and "Foster Garvey PC (Seattle, WA)" in 2025–2026. Foster Garvey was formed in 2019 when Foster Pepper combined with Garvey Schubert Barer *(general reference)*. As a law firm it represents the district under engagement. Under the professional rules Ready cites (RPC 1.13), its client is the district acting through its board, not any one official.

**Via Healthcare Consulting** — A private consulting firm, employer of Karma Bass and Karen Wagner, engaged by the district for board governance work and retreat facilitation. Its exact legal form (corporation, LLC, etc.) is not stated in the source files.

**Washington State Hospital Association (WSHA)** — A private nonprofit trade association of Washington hospitals *(general reference for legal form)*. Its annual conference in Chelan, Washington is why the board held its 2015 and June 29, 2016 meetings off campus there.

**The Port Townsend Leader** — A privately owned weekly newspaper in Port Townsend *(general reference for legal form)*. It published Ready's September 2025 op-ed, "Sunlight Is the Best Medicine for Democracy," quoted in Chapter 11.

**readyforhealthcare.org** — Matt Ready's personal campaign and commissioner website. It is not a hospital publication. It is where he posted the July 2, 2016 Chelan account and recording.

**OpenAI (ChatGPT)** — A private U.S. artificial-intelligence company and its chatbot product *(general reference)*. The 2023 compilation ends with a ChatGPT exchange (Chapter 10).

**Peninsula Health Alliance** — A *proposed* private nonprofit corporation that would have sat above Jefferson Healthcare and OMC. It was never formed. Mentioned only in the Afterword.

## Laws referred to

**Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA), RCW 42.30** — Washington's open-meetings statute. It requires governing bodies to deliberate and act in public and forbids conditions on public attendance other than orderly conduct. Its preamble ("The people, in delegating authority, do not give their public servants the right to decide what is good for the people to know…") is quoted in Ready's 2014 reply to Chair Dressler.

**Public Records Act, RCW 42.56** — Called the "Open Public Record Act" in the 2014 transcript and the "Open Public Records Act" in the 2016 policy text. It governs retention and disclosure of public records. The board's stated worry was that a commissioner's recording would itself be a public record the district had to keep.

**AGO 1998 No. 15** — The Attorney General opinion holding that a county legislative body "may not ban the use of recording devices from the open portion of a meeting held pursuant to the Open Public Meetings Act." Quoted in full in Chapter 3.

**Robert's Rules of Order** — The parliamentary procedure manual the board followed. Ready argues the recording question should have been a simple ruling from the chair on whether recording was in or out of order.

## A Chronology at a Glance

- **May 2013** — Ready announces he is running for hospital commissioner.
- **November 2013** — Elected, Position 3. *(Timeline sources; the exact election night is not in the collected works.)*
- **January 2014** — Takes office.
- **Early 2014** — Before he first records, CEO Glenn and Commissioner Dressler consult attorney Brad Berg. Ready phones Berg. *(Author's recollection, 2026.)*
- **March 19, 2014** — First regular meeting. Ready records. The chair recesses. He stops. *(Transcript.)*
- **March 26–27, 2014** — Ready's letter citing AGO 1998 No. 15; Chair Dressler's reply. *(Documents.)*
- **2015** — Ready records the board's regular meeting in Chelan without objection. *(Author's account, 2016.)*
- **June 29, 2016** — Chelan. DeLeo walks out. The board adjourns rather than continue while recorded. *(Transcript and author's account.)*
- **2016** — The administration obtains a written opinion from Berg's firm. Ready says the full board does not see it until 2021. *(Author's recollection.)*
- **October 14, 2019** — Governance retreat facilitated by Karma Bass. The recording question comes up. *(Transcript.)*
- **December 18, 2019** — Ready's proposed policy fails 3–1 after counsel says he would need to research the question. *(Documents/transcript summary.)*
- **2021** — The 2016 opinion reaches the full board. *(Author's recollection.)*
- **January 14, 2021** — The board unanimously adopts recording-rights language. *(Compilation.)*
- **January 20, 2023** (date as given in the source) — Port Ludlow retreat. The dispute is discussed at length and the facilitator asks that it be declared "complete." *(Transcript.)*
- **2023** — Ready compiles *Recording Fiasco Transcripts with Good Names* and publishes *Journey Through the Boardroom*.
- **2025–2026** — Op-ed, emails, and a bar grievance revisit the episode. *(Author's recollections.)*

title: Part One: 2013–2014 — The Recorder on the Table — Chapter 1. A New Commissioner
text:
## Part One: 2013–2014 — The Recorder on the Table

## Chapter 1. A New Commissioner

Matt Ready did not come to the board as an outsider to the hospital. By the district's official biography, as summarized in his timeline notes, he worked at Jefferson Healthcare for about fifteen years "up until the day he was elected." He worked first in Information Systems (computer technician, application specialist, database administrator, briefly interim director) and from 2007 in the Performance Improvement department, leading improvement workshops. In May 2013, after Occupy Port Townsend, he announced on readyforhealthcare.org that he was running for hospital commissioner. He won Position 3 that November and took office in January 2014.

He later described what he meant to do with the job, and why he began to record:

*[AUTHOR'S RECOLLECTION (LATER) — "Sunlight Is the Best Medicine for Democracy," op-ed submitted to the Port Townsend Leader, September 14, 2025]*
> Winning the Right to Record Soon after taking office in 2014, I began recording board meetings so we could learn from every word, but the CEO and commissioners then in office fiercely opposed it. It took nine years, the arrival of two new commissioners—Kolff and McComas—and a legal opinion the CEO had withheld for five years to confirm what I had argued all along: commissioners and citizens have the absolute right to record public meetings.
>
> Today, the board records on-site meetings but still refuses to record off-site ones, so I do it myself at my own expense. The long fight over something as basic as recording meetings exposed a deep hostility to transparency and set the stage for the next crisis: the Peninsula Health Alliance.

His 2026 grievance to the Washington State Bar Association gives the fullest account of how the question first reached the district's lawyer. It was written twelve years after the fact, and it is his memory of a private phone call:

*[AUTHOR'S RECOLLECTION (LATER) — Grievance narrative concerning attorney Brad Berg, resubmitted June 25, 2026]*
> The origin (2014–2016). The matter began over something deliberately small: whether a commissioner could make an audio recording of a public meeting. Soon after I took office in 2014, I began recording meetings so there would be an accurate record of what was said and decided. Before I first recorded, CEO Mike Glenn and Commissioner Dressler consulted Mr. Berg, the District’s counsel, about the question. I then spoke with Mr. Berg directly, by telephone, to learn his position for myself. He told me, in substance, that I had the right to record the meetings, and that a reasonable solution to the record-keeping question was to provide a copy of each recording to the organization.

No recording or note of that phone call is in the files used for this book. What Berg told Ready is known only from Ready's account.

title: Chapter 2. March 19, 2014 — The Opening Confrontation
text:
## Chapter 2. March 19, 2014 — The Opening Confrontation

Ready's first regular meeting as a commissioner lasted six minutes before it was recessed. The board was meeting at the hospital. Commissioner Jill Buhler was excused. Ready had placed an audio recorder in front of him.

*[TRANSCRIPT — Jefferson Healthcare Board of Commissioners regular meeting, March 19, 2014 (from the 2023 compilation, as reproduced in Appendix D.1 of the author's manuscript)]*
> **Marie Dressler:** …Calling the meeting to order at 3:33. This is Jefferson County Public Hospital District N.2, Board of Commissioners meeting and Commissioner Jill Buhler is excused. Could I ask you what is in front of you? Are you recording this meeting?
>
> **Matt Ready:** Yes. I’m making an audio recording of this meeting to help me remember what has happened.
>
> **Marie Dressler:** Okay. Actually that sounds like a good opening for discussion about doing something like that with one of the concerns with the Public Meetings Act as it is being recorded and the Public Hospital District is responsible for safekeeping…
>
> **Mike Glenn:** I think that there was going to be a discussion at tonight’s meeting about recording board meetings, which I think is a reasonable thing to discuss. There are implications associated with recording board meetings that recording become part of the record… So I think the recommendation from Council is that absent of the hospital doing it, that a board member should not.
>
> **Matt Ready:** Well, based on my research I don’t think that’s accurate. I mean, this is a public meeting, citizens have a certain right to record these meetings; I don’t surrender that right because I’m a Commissioner… I would disagree with that assessment of what is legal, or that this constitutes a board act, this is an act as a private citizen.
>
> **Mike Glenn:** Well, it might be an act of a private citizen but because of your — because you’re a board member, just like the notes you take at a board meeting, they are subject to the Open Public Record Act, so that any tape that you record is also subject to that act, so it becomes part of the record and it’s the recommendation from Council looking after the interests of the organization that if Jefferson Healthcare begins to record our meetings, that it be done though Administration so that we have the tape, we have the record, we can properly store it…
>
> **Matt Ready:** Is the Council recommending me not record meetings?
>
> **Mike Glenn:** Until we have a policy and a procedure to make sure we can manage that recording in compliance with the Open Public Record Act, that we don’t do it, because it’s discretionary…
>
> **Matt Ready:** I appreciate the recommendation of Council, but I’m going to continue recording the meeting. I think it’s a perfectly appropriate decision and I would completely support the board if we wanted to officially do it and I’m happy to give, if you feel like you need a copy to store for seven years, I’m happy to provide that.
>
> **Mike Glenn:** Well, it’s not like I feel like it. The law would require it, and the recommendation from Council is that if a recording is made on behalf of the organization and as a Commissioner you would be making it on behalf of the organization, that we have our own recording.
>
> **Marie Dressler:** So I will recess this board meeting at 3:39 to see if we can locate a recording — some recording device, and if not we will just have to schedule a special meeting. Thank you.
>
> [Pause]
>
> **Marie Dressler:** At 3:43 I will reconvene the meeting [inaudible] Hospital District N. 2, I continue our meeting.
>
> **Tony Deleo:** Madam Chairman, if you would [unclear] that Commissioner Ready is no longer recording the meeting.

The compilation does not record Ready's own words at the moment he switched off the device. The meeting went on only after Commissioner DeLeo confirmed, on the record, that Ready "is no longer recording the meeting."

Three positions were already on the table in that first exchange, and they barely changed over the next seven years. The CEO, relaying counsel, said a commissioner's recording becomes the district's record and the district should control it. Ready said recording an open meeting is a citizen's right that a commissioner does not give up. And Ready offered, in the same breath, to hand over a copy for the district to keep for seven years.

title: Chapter 3. The Letters — March 26–27, 2014
text:
## Chapter 3. The Letters — March 26–27, 2014

A week later Ready put his offer in writing.

*[DOCUMENT — Letter from Matthew Ready to CEO Mike Glenn and Chair Marie Dressler, March 26, 2014 (excerpts as reproduced in the compilation)]*
> Dear Mike,
>
> I would like for us to work together to avoid any further public confrontations or drawn out conflicts over the issue of audio recordings of commission public meetings.
>
> To best do my job as a hospital commissioner I require a complete record of our public meetings. I require this complete record to be in my possession the moment our public meetings conclude so that I might immediately review any portion of the meeting events and begin considering next steps…
>
> I believe the simplest solution is that I record the meetings on my personal recording device and immediately provide a copy of the file to administration after the meeting. I could simply walk over to the commission office, plug in my usb cable, and upload the file to a directory on the file server. The file is already dated by the software. The hospital Information Technology department keeps backups of all files on the file server. If anyone ever requests one of the audio files from a meeting, then someone could simply copy the file to a thumb drive for the person…
>
> As you noted, any handwritten notes a hospital commissioner makes during a public meeting is subject public records standards. Audio recordings, are simply a form of note taking. We may need to refine it, but the policy regarding commissioner notetaking you described is already in place and as long as I make my recordings available in a timely manner, we appear to be keeping with the policy we already have…
>
> We have another public meeting on 4/16/2014. I would like to record this meeting. Please let me know if my recording the meeting will result in yourself and/or the board chair delaying the meeting progress on the agenda, recessing the meeting, or adjourning the meeting as happened at the 3/19/2014 meeting…
>
> Respectfully,
>
> Matthew Ready

He attached the Attorney General's opinion:

*[DOCUMENT — Washington State Attorney General Opinion AGO 1998 No. 15 (excerpt attached to the letter)]*
> A county is subject to the Open Public Meetings Act which generally requires that meetings of the governing body be open to the public and that no conditions precedent to attendance by the public, except for orderly conduct, may be imposed. Therefore, a county legislative body may not ban the use of recording devices from the open portion of a meeting held pursuant to the Open Public Meetings Act. The county legislative body may impose restrictions on the use of recording devices, but only to the extent necessary to preserve the orderly conduct of the meeting.

The chair answered the next day.

*[DOCUMENT — Email from Chair Marie Dressler to Matt Ready, March 27, 2014]*
> Hello Matt,
>
> Actually, audio recording of Board meetings is a Board decision.
>
> At the conclusion of our last meeting we, the Board, asked Mike to develop a policy, procedure and recording methodology to present to the Board for our review and consideration. At this time, the board can then discuss and take action, if appropriate.
>
> Mike and I participated in a teleconference with counsel and were made aware of the legal implications to the District related to recording Board meetings. If we are going to do this, then we are going to do it correctly. Interestingly, according to counsel, it is not common for a Public Hospital District to record it’s board meetings.
>
> Based on this, Matt, it would certainly be best if you chose not to exercise any right you have, to record the 4/16 meeting and allow the Board the time and space to make a thoughtful and deliberate decision on this issue.
>
> Marie Dressler Board Chair

The rest of the exchange survives only in summary. The compilation reports:

*[DOCUMENT (SUMMARY IN THE COMPILATION)]*
> The author replied citing the OPMA’s preamble — “The people, in delegating authority, do not give their public servants the right to decide what is good for the people to know and what is not good for them to know” — and asked for the name and contact information of the attorney whose advice was being cited. Chair Dressler responded that the consultation Matt had requested would be “solely and totally at your own expense.”

Ready's later analysis (Section 3E.1 of his manuscript) adds that the chair gave only a partial name for the attorney, "a Seattle attorney, identified later as Brad Berg of Foster Pepper." That identification is the author's, made later. *(SECONDARY.)*

By 2016 the board was recording its own meetings at the hospital. The policy Ready quotes in 2016 provides for "official audio recordings of all open public meetings" that "may be made by board designated staff." The source files do not say exactly when that policy was adopted. The open question was what happened when the board did not record and a commissioner did.

title: Part Two: 2015–2016 — Chelan — Chapter 4. June 29, 2016 — The Walkout in Chelan
text:
## Part Two: 2015–2016 — Chelan

## Chapter 4. June 29, 2016 — The Walkout in Chelan

Each June the board met in regular session in Chelan, Washington, during the Washington State Hospital Association's annual conference. The board's own recording equipment did not travel. In 2015 Ready recorded that meeting on his handheld recorder, and by his account nobody objected. A year later it was different.

## The transcript

*[TRANSCRIPT — Jefferson Healthcare Board of Commissioners off-site regular meeting, Chelan, Washington, June 29, 2016 (from the 2023 compilation, as reproduced in Appendix D.4)]*
> **Matt Ready:** So… just so you know.
>
> **Tony Deleo:** We’re not going to record this meeting Matt.
>
> **Matt Ready:** I’m recording it.
>
> **Tony Deleo:** No you’re not.
>
> **Marie Dressler:** That’s not our policy, is it?
>
> **Kees Kolff:** Wait, is this an official meeting?
>
> **Marie Dressler:** It’s an official board meeting, but our policy states that we record when we’re in our normal board situation, board meeting room at the hospital.
>
> **Kees Kolff:** There’s nothing that prohibits Matt from recording it.
>
> **Tony Deleo:** Yes there is. It makes it official record.
>
> **Kees Kolff:** There should be an official record if it’s an official meeting.
>
> **Mike Glenn:** Well, there is a legal opinion that recommends to not do this actually…
>
> **Tony Deleo:** Are you still recording?
>
> **Matt Ready:** I’m recording the meeting.
>
> **Tony Deleo:** Okay.

## What Ready saw

The compilation then breaks from the transcript into Ready's own first-person account of the moment DeLeo stood up:

*[AUTHOR'S ACCOUNT — First-person narrative in the 2023 compilation (written after the fact; the compilation calls it contemporaneous)]*
> I was seated to his right with at least one person in between us, but nonetheless, I remember my surprise at his actions. When someone is angry with you and they suddenly rise from the table, you don’t know what will happen next. My brain immediately started evaluating possibilities. I must admit, my body experienced a shot of extra adrenaline instinctively, since I suppose at a primal level, I perceived some sort of violence towards me was possible. I saw my recorder sitting on the table out in front of me and thought, “Is he going to grab at my recorder?”… So I look at my recorder and prepare myself to casually reach out and take hold of it if Commissioner Deleo makes a move in my direction… In any case, Commissioner Deleo did not make any move in my direction, instead he stepped away from the table and walked briskly towards the door and said:

## The transcript resumes

> **Tony Deleo:** See you guys later! Let me know if he turns it off.
>
> [Commissioner Deleo exits the room.]
>
> **Jill Buhler:** This is a little counterproductive. Do you really want to do this Matt?
>
> **Matt Ready:** Sorry, my stress level is very high right now, so it’s hard for me to speak. I did not expect a massive conflict over this again. I didn’t think you guys would be surprised. I recorded last year’s meeting, if you recall, so I’ve told you before, I cannot actually remember everything that is said at these meetings, and it’s important to me that we take what we say here seriously, and we’re held accountable for what we say here, and the only way to do that is to have an accurate record of these meetings, and so I record the meetings.

The compilation summarizes what followed:

*[DOCUMENT (SUMMARY IN THE COMPILATION)]*
> DeLeo subsequently moved a motion to “forbid Commissioner Ready from recording this meeting.” The motion died for lack of clear procedural support. A motion to conclude the meeting passed instead. The board adjourned rather than continuing with the recording in progress.

Ready's later analysis adds two exchanges that are not in the Appendix D excerpt. It says Kolff asked whether handing the recording to the board secretary right away would resolve the concern, that Chair Jill Buhler answered, "It does not, because it does not follow policy," and that Kolff then moved to conclude. *(SECONDARY: from Section 3E.1. The underlying transcript lines are not in the files used for this book.)*

## Ready's public account, three days later

On July 2, 2016 Ready posted the recording with this explanation. It is his contemporaneous account, and the only document in this book that quotes the board's recording policy in force at the time.

*[AUTHOR'S ACCOUNT (CONTEMPORANEOUS) — "Jefferson Healthcare Commission Meeting – 06/29/2016," readyforhealthcare.org, July 2, 2016]*
> In Chelan, Wa the Jefferson Healthcare Board of commissioners met in regular session following the annual WSHA conference. Since our normal audio recording equipment does not travel with us, I recorded the meeting with my own handheld digital recorder.
>
> To my surprise, the majority of my fellow commissioners took exception to me recording the meeting. When I refused to stop recording the meeting, they decided to conclude the meeting rather than continue. You can hear commissioner De Leo leave the meeting in protest of my recording. He later rejoins the meeting at about the 5:50 mark.
>
> As I say during this brief meeting, I make sure a recording of all meetings is made because I feel it is essential for me to do my job. Everyone in that room needs to be held accountable for what we say- because what we say and do matters. Without a complete record of the meetings, too much time can be spent arguing about what we agreed to or said in the past, rather than discussing actually important and difficult subjects.
>
> I truly thought this board was done debating the issue of recording our public meetings. A year earlier, I recorded our regular meeting in Chelan, WA in the exact same manner, but last year none of the objections raised during this year’s meeting were raised. The recording a year ago is here.
>
> If you listen to the recording the following are the two objections raised as best I can discern.
>
> 1. A hospital lawyer has advised that if a commissioner records the meeting, then the recording may be argued to be an official record and therefore needs to be archived with other recordings. The resolution to this point, as I say in the meeting and have said since this point was first raised two years ago: I will give the recording to the hospital to store with the other recordings.
>
> 2. The second objection seems to be referring to the board policy on recording meetings which was intentionally drafted in a way to give the board the freedom to not record a meeting if it so chooses. The reason for this flexibility was to allow the board to meet with people off campus who might be disinclined to meet with us if we insisted on recording the meeting. If we insisted on recording such meetings, we might hamper our ability to serve our district if our access to elected officials became more limited. The policy in place at the time of this meeting reads as follows:
>
> In addition to the written minutes of regular and special meetings, official audio recordings of all open public meetings may be made by board designated staff and said recordings will be processed, retained and made available in accordance with the Open Public Records Act.
>
> Since this meeting was not with any outside entities and was merely a meeting of our board off campus, there was no reason for it not to be recorded. So I recorded it as I did the meeting in Chelan the year prior. Moreover, though this policy gives the board the choice to record a meeting or not, it does not take away every individual commissioners right to record the meeting if they so choose. I continue to be unsure exactly why my fellow commissioners decided to suddenly raise these objections and refused to continue the meeting while it was recorded. Below is the recording I made.

## After the recorder was off

Ten years later Ready added one more line to the record: something he says was said after the meeting ended, when nothing was recording. It is not on the 2016 post or in the transcript compilation. He states it from memory.

## Chapter 5. The Opinion in the Drawer — 2016

Sometime in 2016, after Chelan, the administration asked the district's law firm for a written answer to the question the board kept fighting about. The letter itself is not in the files used for this book. What we know about it comes from two people who disagree about what it meant: Ready, and, years later, CEO Glenn (Chapter 9).

Ready's account:

*[AUTHOR'S RECOLLECTION (LATER) — Grievance narrative concerning attorney Brad Berg, 2026]*
> The written opinion, and five years of silence. In 2016, the administration obtained a written legal opinion from Mr. Berg’s firm addressing the same question, but the administration did not reveal that opinion to the full board until 2021, when the board voted to obtain a written legal opinion on the matter. That written opinion was consistent with the position Mr. Berg had given me by phone. Yet the full board — including me — was never told the opinion existed, and was denied access to it, despite my repeated requests for written legal answers between 2016 and 2021. It had been shared with at least one commissioner before 2021. For five years, a written legal answer to the very question we were fighting about sat in the administration’s hands while the board it would have settled was kept from it.
>
> The contradiction. Throughout those years, up to 2021, I repeatedly asked the board to clarify the law — because interfering with a commissioner’s recording appeared to violate statute, and the board urgently needed a lawful and ethical method, consistent with Robert’s Rules of Order, for handling the situation. Mr. Berg never appeared before the full board to clarify the law on the matter — the very step that, once finally taken in 2021, opened the door to an immediate and sensible resolution. For years the commissioners, the people legally responsible for the District, were denied access to the legal answer, at a cost measured in wasted time, wasted energy, and lost trust.

In the same narrative he sets limits on his claim:

> What I do and do not allege. I want to be precise about the limits of this. I do not allege that Mr. Berg’s advice in 2014 or 2016 was wrong; by my account it was correct and matched the written opinion. I do not allege that preparing an opinion for the administration was itself improper. And I do not claim to know everything Mr. Berg was told about how his position was being represented to the board. What I ask the Office to examine is narrower: whether a lawyer whose client is the full elected board of a public agency meets his duties of candor and loyalty when his advice is withheld from that board for years and contradicted to their faces, and he does not act to correct the record with the board directly. The duty to set the client straight arises when counsel knows or should know his advice is being distorted to the client’s detriment. Whether Mr. Berg knew is a question for the Office; that the distortion occurred, and that he did not convene the full board to correct it, I can attest.

His accounts give two different lengths for the dispute. The 2025 op-ed says the CEO withheld the opinion "for five years" and counts the whole fight as nine years. The 2026 grievance says the conflict "consumed five years" and ended in 2021. Both are his words. The difference is which span he is counting.

## Part Four: 2021 — How It Ended

## Chapter 8. The Letter Comes Out; the Board Votes

The end came quickly once the 2016 letter reached the full board. By Ready's later account, the board had voted to obtain a written legal opinion on recording, and the existing letter then surfaced. At Port Ludlow he recalled the explanation he was given: "Jill found the opinion on her desk."

*[AUTHOR'S RECOLLECTION (LATER) — Grievance narrative concerning attorney Brad Berg, 2026]*
> How it ended (2021). Only in 2021 was the written opinion finally provided to the full board. Once we could simply read it, the board promptly adopted a sensible policy on recording with a personal device and voted to move on. A conflict that had consumed five years ended within weeks of the board being allowed to see the legal answer that had existed since 2016.

The compilation records the vote:

*[DOCUMENT — Board policy action, January 14, 2021 (as reproduced in Appendix D.7)]*
> After seven years of dispute, the Jefferson Healthcare Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to add language to its policy book stating that any commissioner who independently records an open public meeting would promptly provide a copy to the district for public records storage. The two principles all members of the board now endorsed:
>
> A commissioner has the right to record any open public meeting of the commission whether regular or special session, on site or offsite (as do all residents of the United States).
>
> No one can (or should try to) prohibit a recording of anyone in an open public meeting, even if they personally object to the recording.

The two principles are, in substance, what AGO 1998 No. 15 had said and what Ready had cited in 2014. Commissioner McComas, speaking at Port Ludlow, called it the point where "we revised our board, to stiffen up our policy around audio recording… we made it even better policy in 2021."

One practical gap stayed open. In his 2025 op-ed Ready writes that "the board records on-site meetings but still refuses to record off-site ones, so I do it myself at my own expense" (Chapter 1).

title: Chapter 10. The 2023 Compilation and the Machine's Version
text:
## Chapter 10. The 2023 Compilation and the Machine's Version

In 2023 Ready gathered the transcripts, letters, and his own notes into one document, *Recording Fiasco Transcripts with Good Names (pre-AI compilation)*. His manuscript describes it as "the canonical record." That full compilation is not among the files used for this book. Every 2014–2021 transcript quoted here comes from the selections he reprinted in Appendix D of his 2026 manuscript. The same year he published *Journey Through the Boardroom: An Insider's Perspective on Hospital Governance*, which by his 2025 account documents the retreats as well.

The compilation ends with a coda. In it, Ready asked ChatGPT to write a news story about the seven-year dispute. His manuscript describes what happened:

*[AUTHOR'S ACCOUNT — Note on the 2023 ChatGPT coda (Appendix D.8 of the author's manuscript)]*
> The 2023 compilation of the Recording Fiasco transcripts closes with the author asking ChatGPT to write a news story summarizing the seven-year dispute. ChatGPT initially produced a plausible-but-mostly-accurate paraphrase. When the author asked it to attribute quotes more carefully to the correct speakers, ChatGPT instead generated a completely fabricated story about a “John Smith of ABC Company” announcing a merger with “XYZ Inc.” This is preserved as the closing item in the 2023 compilation. The author intended it as wry commentary on AI hallucination. It also functions, in retrospect, as a structurally apt closing image: the moment a human-authored verification record was handed to a system designed to summarize, the system invented a different story entirely and reported it with confidence. The shadow tree mechanism reproduced in real time, in machine form, in a single conversation. The verbatim record preserved in this appendix is the corrective.

The ChatGPT text itself is not in the files used for this book and is not reproduced.

## Chapter 11. The Fight in Later Accounts

The recording dispute kept coming back in Ready's writing as the origin of the conflict that followed. These are his recollections and characterizations, written in 2025 and 2026 during a different dispute.

## To the facilitator, April 2025

When Karma Bass asked him in April 2025 to take part in a private pre-retreat interview, he declined and explained why:

*[AUTHOR'S RECOLLECTION (LATER) — Email from Matt Ready to Karma Bass, April 3, 2025 (excerpt)]*
> Thank you for your message. I need to respectfully decline the invitation for a private phone or audio interview related to the upcoming board retreat.
>
> I have serious concerns about the confidentiality and legal implications of such a conversation, especially given your past role facilitating the 2019 board retreat. At that retreat, the board failed to reckon with the fact that a critical 2016 legal opinion—affirming a commissioner’s right to record public meetings—had been withheld from me and the public for years. I documented this entire episode in my book, Journey Through the Boardroom, including the moment during the retreat when I stated on the record that what Mike Glenn and Brad Berg had done could be considered fraud. Instead of allowing that conversation to continue, you intervened and asked, “Are you a lawyer?”—effectively shutting down the discussion. That moment could have opened the door to transparency and healing. Instead, it served to protect those in power and bury the issue.

(On the placement of "Are you a lawyer?" in 2019, see the note at the end of Chapter 6.)

## To the voters, September 2025

The op-ed quoted in Chapter 1 counts "nine years" from 2014 to the right-to-record victory. That would place the end around 2023, the year of the Port Ludlow retreat and the compilation, rather than at the 2021 vote.

## To the bar, June 2026

In his grievance concerning attorney Berg, Ready presents the recording episode as the first instance of a pattern in which counsel's advice reached the board only through the administration. He calls it "The same pattern, eleven years later":

*[AUTHOR'S RECOLLECTION (LATER) — Grievance narrative concerning attorney Brad Berg, 2026]*
> The same pattern, eleven years later. The 2025 events trace the identical shape. Mr. Berg’s advice again reached the board through the CEO and chair rather than directly: I was told that the chair, the CEO, and Mr. Berg had discussed my concerns and that Mr. Berg had said the board’s actions were lawful. When I asked the board to test that advice with independent counsel, his authority was again invoked to refuse — one commissioner calling him “the definitive person on this particular type of issue” who had “actually written the code that we follow,” and the chair stating that counsel “has said that nothing we have done is illegal” and was “preeminent in this discussion.” And again, Mr. Berg never sat with the full board to let his advice be questioned in the open. The recording episode shows this was not a one-time lapse under pressure. It is how counsel has operated with this board across two separate controversies, eleven years apart.

That grievance is an allegation submitted for review, not a finding. This book takes no position on it.

title: Afterword: How Long Was It?
text:
## Afterword: How Long Was It?

The sources give three lengths for the Recording Fiasco, and all three are the author's:

- **Seven years** (2014–2021): the 2023 compilation, the ChatGPT coda, Section 3E.1, and Ready's own words at Port Ludlow ("distracted me for seven years"), echoed by the facilitator.
- **Nine years**: the September 2025 op-ed ("It took nine years").
- **Five years**: the time the 2016 opinion went unseen by the full board, in the op-ed and the 2026 grievance ("A conflict that had consumed five years ended within weeks").

They count different things: the whole fight, the fight plus its aftermath, and the life of the withheld letter. This book uses 2014–2021 for the dispute and 2023 for its last recorded discussion. In 2025 Ready wrote that the episode "set the stage for the next crisis: the Peninsula Health Alliance." That story, a proposed alliance with Olympic Medical Center, is told in his separate book *Project Driftwood*.
